lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto took over on December 20, 1971 as the country's first Civilian Martial Law Administrator.
  • The nationalization of industries was announced on January 2, 1972, and Martial Law ended in April 1972.
  • The 1973 Constitution was drawn up by a committee of 25 members of the National Assembly.
  • After taking power in 1977, General Zia-ul-Haq promised to hold elections within 90 days; he became President in September 1978.
  • Prime Minister Muhammad Khan Junejo announced the Five-points Programme.
  • Benazir Bhutto took the vote of confidence on December 12, 1988 and launched the Peoples' Works Programme.
  • Nawaz Sharif became Prime Minister for the first time on November 6, 1990.
  • Pakistan became a nuclear power on May 28, 1998.

Solved Exercises

Exercise I: Choose the right answer to the following questions

Q: 1. When did Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto become the first Martial Law Administrator of the country?

Options: (a) 16th December 1971 (b) 20th December 1971 (c) 22th December 1971 (d) 23th December 1971

Correct answer: 20th December 1971

Q: 2. When was the nationalization of industries announced?

Options: (a) 2th January 1972 (b) 12th January 1972 (c) 16th January 1972 (d) 20th January 1972

Correct answer: 2th January 1972

Q: 3. When was the Martial Law ended during the Bhutto regime?

Options: (a) February 1972 (b) March 1972 (c) April 1972 (d) August 1972

Correct answer: April 1972

Q: 4. What was the strength of the National Assembly Committee tasked with drawing the 1973 Constitution?

Options: (a) 15 (b) 20 (c) 22 (d) 25

Correct answer: 25

Q: 5. After the assumption of power Zia-ul-Haq promised to hold elections within how many days?

Options: (a) 80 (b) 90 (c) 95 (d) 120

Correct answer: 90

Q: 6. When did General Zia assume the position of President?

Options: (a) July 1977 (b) March 1978 (c) July 1978 (d) September 1978

Correct answer: September 1978

Q: 7. Which Ordinance did Zia promulgate on June 20, 1980?

Options: (a) Labor Reforms (b) Islamic Hudood and Tazeraat (c) Zakat and Ushar (d) Zakat Foundation

Correct answer: Zakat and Ushar

Q: 8. Which Prime Minister announced the Five-points Programme?

Options: (a) Benazir Bhutto (b) Muhammad Khan Junejo (c) Nawaz Sharif (d) Ghulam Mustafa Jatoi

Correct answer: Muhammad Khan Junejo

Q: 9. When did Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto took vote of confidence from the National Assembly?

Options: (a) 2nd December 1988 (b) 8th December 1988 (c) 10th December 1988 (d) 12th December 1988

Correct answer: 12th December 1988

Q: 10. Who launched the Peoples' Works Programme?

Options: (a) Prime Minister Muhammad Khan Junejo (b) Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto (c) Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif (d) President Ghulam Ishaq Khan

Correct answer: Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto

Q: 11. When did Nawaz Sharif become Prime Minister for the first time?

Options: (a) 6th November 1990 (b) 6th December 1990 (c) 6th January 1991 (d) 6th February 1992

Correct answer: 6th November 1990

Q: 12. Who launched the National Finance Commission Award?

Options: (a) Benazir Bhutto (b) Nawaz Sharif (c) Mairaj Khalid (d) Farooq Laghari

Correct answer: Nawaz Sharif

Q: 13. Why is 28th May 1998 important in the history of Pakistan?

Options: (a) Nawaz Sharif came to power (b) Martial Law was imposed (c) Self-Employment Scheme was launched (d) Pakistan became a nuclear power

Correct answer: Pakistan became a nuclear power

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The nationalization programme was announced in 1972 through an Ordinance; twenty industries were nationalized and foreign enterprises were not interfered with.
  • The Federal Shariat Court came into existence during Zia-ul-Haq's Islamization; each High Court was to have a Shariat Bench of three judges.
  • Wafaqi Mohtasib means the Federal Ombudsman; announced in June 1981, it is a non-political office with a tenure of four years.
  • The Geneva Talks concerned the Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan; Soviet evacuation was to start by May 15, 1988 and about three and a half million Afghan refugees were in Pakistan.
  • Junejo's Five-points Programme was declared on December 31, 1985 and spanned four years.
  • Musharraf's local government plan of 2000 created a three-tier structure of Union, Tehsil/Town and District Councils, implemented by the National Reconstruction Bureau.
  • Under the Local Government Ordinance 2005, the members of the Union Council and the number of Councilors were reduced from 21 to 13.

Solved Exercises

Exercise II: Write short answers to the following questions

Q: 1. When was the nationalization programme announced and which industries were nationalized?

Ans: The nationalization programme was announced in 1972 through an Ordinance. The industries nationalized under it were the iron and steel industry, basic metallurgy, heavy engineering, automobile and tractor assembling plants, heavy electrical engineering plants and oil and gas refineries. In all, twenty such industries in these sectors were nationalized. While the policy of nationalization was carried out with regard to domestic investment, foreign enterprises operating in the country were not interfered with.

Q: 2. When did the Federal Sharia Court come into existence?

Ans: The Federal Shariat Court came into existence during General Zia-ul-Haq's Islamization process, when the 1973 Constitution was amended for the enforcement of the Islamic way of life. Under this amendment, each High Court was to have a Shariat Bench consisting of three judges, and the Supreme Court of Pakistan an Appellate Shariat Bench of three judges. This court had due powers and could annul any law that it deemed un-Islamic. The verdicts of the Shariat Benches were binding upon all, including the President of the Republic, while an appeal against a verdict could be made in the Appellate Shariat Bench of the Supreme Court.

Q: 3. What is meant by Wafaqi Mohtasib?

Ans: Wafaqi Mohtasib means the Federal Ombudsman. In June 1981 Zia-ul-Haq announced the establishment of this institution for the protection of citizens' rights, since accountability is an important aspect of Islamic society and ensures the rule of law, the provision of justice and the promotion of social equality. The office of the Wafaqi Mohtasib is non-political and non-partisan, and its tenure is four years. Anyone who feels aggrieved by any government official or government department can seek justice by complaining in writing on plain paper and sending it by ordinary post to the Wafaqi Mohtasib.

Q: 4. Write a short note on the Geneva Talks.

Ans: The Geneva Talks concerned the Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan. After Mikhail Gorbachev, the new Soviet leader, showed a flexible attitude, the issue came under the mediation of the United Nations in December 1987, and on January 10, 1988 Gorbachev announced that if the problem was resolved by 15 March, Soviet forces would start evacuating by May 15, 1988. There was a visible discord between Zia-ul-Haq and Prime Minister Muhammad Khan Junejo: Junejo was prepared to sign the Geneva Accord by March 1, while Zia insisted that the establishment of an interim government in Afghanistan was essential for lasting peace and for the repatriation of some three and a half million Afghan refugees. In spite of these reservations, Junejo put his signature on the Geneva Accord.

Q: 5. Explain the Five-points Programme of Prime Minister Junejo.

Ans: On December 31, 1985 Prime Minister Muhammad Khan Junejo declared his Five-points Programme, which spanned over four years. Its points were: (1) based on the ideology of Pakistan, the establishment of a stable Islamic democratic system; (2) the establishment of a just economic system for ensuring the social wellbeing of the people and the eradication of unemployment; (3) the eradication of illiteracy from the country, preparing the nation for the challenges of the modern age of science and technology; (4) the eradication of corruption and injustice and the provision of justice and social security to the masses; and (5) the surety of national security and sovereignty through strong defence and a balanced, non-aligned foreign policy.

Q: 6. What do you know about local governments?

Ans: On March 23, 2000 General Pervez Musharraf, as Chief Executive, proposed a comprehensive plan for the devolution of power to local government institutions, so that the masses could participate in the political process at the grassroots level, and the National Reconstruction Bureau was established to implement it. On August 14, 2000 he announced a three-tier structure consisting of the Union Council, the Tehsil/Town Council and the District Council. The elections, held stepwise, commenced in December 2000 and were completed in July 2001. The Nazims and Naib Nazims of the Union Councils were elected directly by the people, while those of the Tehsil and District Councils were elected indirectly. Thirty percent of seats at each level were specified for women, and seats were also reserved for minorities, labourers and farmers. The posts of Deputy Commissioner at the district level and of Commissioner at the divisional level, and even the Divisions themselves, were abolished, and the District Nazim headed the district administration.

Q: 7. Write a note on the Local Government Ordinance 2005.

Ans: The Local and District Governments completed their tenure in June 2005. Before holding new local government elections, their rules were amended in consultation with the Provincial Assemblies, and a new Local Government Ordinance 2005 was promulgated. Under this Ordinance, the members of the Union Council and the number of Councilors were reduced from 21 to 13.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Bhutto's reforms included economic, labour, educational and agricultural reforms, and the nationalization of industries, banks and life insurance companies.
  • Under the 1972 agricultural reforms, the land ceiling was reduced to 150 acres irrigated and 300 acres arid land.
  • The 1973 Constitution is a written federal constitution of 280 articles, enforced on August 14, 1973; an amendment needs a two-thirds majority of the total membership of each House.
  • Zia enforced the Islamic Hudood and Ta'zeerat on February 10, 1979 and promulgated the Zakat and Ushr Ordinance on June 20, 1980, deducting Zakat at 2.5 percent from bank deposits.
  • Zia formed the Majlis-e-Shura in December 1981 with fifty members and announced the Wafaqi Mohtasib in June 1981.
  • Benazir Bhutto took oath as Prime Minister on December 2, 1988; her first government was dissolved on August 6, 1990 and her second on November 5, 1996 under Article 58(2)B.
  • Nawaz Sharif's first government announced the National Finance Commission Award and formed IRSA after the 1991 Indus water agreement between the provinces.
  • Musharraf took over on October 12, 1999 as Chief Executive, became President on June 20, 2001, issued the Legal Framework Order on August 21, 2002, and resigned on August 18, 2008.

Solved Exercises

Exercise III: Give comprehensive answers to the following questions

Q: 1. Write a comprehensive note on the reforms introduced by the government of Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto.

Ans: Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto took over on December 20, 1971 as the country's first Civilian Martial Law Administrator and later worked as Prime Minister. His main reforms were: (1) Economic Reforms: essential commodities were subsidized; farmers were provided seeds, fertilizers and tractors on subsidized rates and agricultural produce was procured at preferential rates. The pay and benefits of government servants were revised, uniformity was ensured by introducing 22 scales, loan facilities were provided, pensions were increased, and the children of low-salary employees were exempted from fees at state-run institutions. (2) Labour Reforms: labour legislation was enacted for the first time in the history of Pakistan. Workers were entitled to free medical care and compensation in case of injury, the right to overtime and bonus was made mandatory, old age pension and group insurance were made obligatory, and workers were protected against summary dismissal. (3) Industries: an Ordinance in 1972 nationalized twenty industries including iron and steel, basic metallurgy, heavy engineering, automobile and tractor assembling, heavy electrical engineering and oil and gas refineries. (4) Life Insurance and Banking: all life insurance companies were nationalized on March 19, 1972 and merged to form the State Life Insurance Corporation in November 1972; all banks were nationalized and put under the control of the State Bank of Pakistan in May 1972. (5) Educational Reforms: educational institutions were nationalized and free education was provided in them, though the policy failed to attain its objectives because some high-standard institutions were left in private hands. (6) Agricultural Reforms: on March 1, 1972 the upper limit of landownership was reduced from 500 acres of irrigated and 1000 acres of arid land to 150 acres irrigated and 300 acres arid; excess land was distributed free among the peasants, eviction of tenants was prohibited, the tenant's right to purchase was given primacy, and the supply of seeds and irrigation water was made the owner's responsibility.

Q: 2. What are the main points of the 1973 Constitution?

Ans: The 1973 Constitution was drafted by a committee of twenty-five elected members of the National Assembly and was enforced in the country on August 14, 1973. Its salient features are: (1) Federal Constitution: it adheres to the principles of federalism and applies to all four provinces, the federal capital Islamabad, FATA and the Northern Areas (now Gilgit Baltistan). (2) Written Constitution: it is a written document having 280 articles. (3) Parliamentary: the Prime Minister, the head of the government, is a member of the Parliament, elected by and responsible to it; the President is the constitutional head of state. (4) Bicameral Legislature: the Parliament has two houses; representation in the National Assembly is on population basis while all provinces have equal representation in the Senate. (5) Fundamental Rights: the Constitution recognized the fundamental rights of the people, and the legislature is denied any right to enact legislation that contravenes them. (6) Constitutional Amendment: an amendment bill can be initiated in any House but must be passed by at least two-thirds majority of the total membership in each House, so the Constitution is neither very rigid nor very flexible. (7) Independent Judiciary: the Constitution guarantees the independence of the judiciary and lays down strict procedures for the appointment and removal of judges of the superior courts. (8) Direct Election: the National Assembly and all Provincial Assemblies are elected for five years through direct votes. (9) National Language: Urdu is recognized as the national language, while the Constitution also guarantees work for the promotion of regional languages.

Q: 3. Give a detailed account of the efforts made by Zia for the enforcement of Islamic laws in Pakistan.

Ans: Soon after taking charge, Zia-ul-Haq proclaimed the enforcement of Islamic Hudood and Ta'zeerat on February 10, 1979, under which punishments prescribed by Shariah for drinking, adultery, theft and false allegation were enforced. His other Islamization steps were: (1) Zakat and Ushr Ordinance: promulgated on June 20, 1980, authorizing the government to deduct Zakat from all bank deposits at the rate of 2.5 percent. (2) Zakat Foundation: in February 1982 the Federal Government established the National Zakat Foundation, with one hundred million rupees allocated initially, to train those deserving Zakat so as to end their dependency on it. (3) Federal Shariat Court: the 1973 Constitution was amended so that each High Court had a Shariat Bench of three judges and the Supreme Court an Appellate Shariat Bench, which could annul any law deemed un-Islamic. (4) Blasphemy Act: Article 298 was amended so that anyone guilty of blasphemy towards the Righteous Caliphs, the family of the Prophet (PBUH) and the Companions could get up to three years of rigorous imprisonment or fine or both. (5) Pakistan Studies and Islamiyat were made compulsory subjects up to degree level in all educational institutions, while non-Muslims were allowed to take Ethics in place of Islamiyat. (6) Ihteram-e-Ramazan Ordinance: promulgated in 1981, it proscribed smoking, eating and drinking by Muslims in public places during Ramazan, punishable by three months' imprisonment or fine or both; in 1984 Salat Committees were also established. (7) Wafaqi Mohtasib: the Federal Ombudsman institution was announced in June 1981 for accountability and protection of citizens' rights. (8) Majlis-e-Shura: formed in December 1981 with fifty members to forge better links between the government and the masses and to suggest steps leading to an Islamic society. (9) Interest-free Banking: steps were taken that led to the introduction of interest-free banking in all the banks, to free the economic system from usury.

Q: 4. Write a note on both the governments of Benazir Bhutto.

Ans: First Term (1988-90): The Pakistan Peoples' Party emerged from the 1988 elections as the party with the largest number of seats in the National Assembly. Benazir Bhutto was invited to form the government on December 1, 1988, took oath as Prime Minister on December 2, 1988 and got the vote of confidence on December 12; it was the first time in the modern history of the Islamic world that a Muslim woman became head of the government. Her message was of unity, peace, freedom and hope. An accord was signed with the Muhajir Qaumi Movement; the National Press Trust was dissolved, making Pakistan Television and Radio Pakistan autonomous; political prisoners were released and the ban on trade unions was lifted. On December 31, 1988 she and the Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi agreed not to attack each other's nuclear installations. On April 23, 1989 she inaugurated the Peoples' Works Programme in Peshawar for social welfare and development at the grassroots level. Her government remained in confrontation with the Islami Jamhuri Ittehad government in Punjab, and on August 6, 1990 President Ghulam Ishaq Khan dissolved the National Assembly on charges of corruption, misuse of power and undermining democratic norms; Ghulam Mustafa Jatoi became Caretaker Prime Minister. Second Term (1993-96): Benazir took oath as Prime Minister for the second time on October 19, 1993. Her government's priorities included reducing unemployment, improving literacy, eliminating load shedding, improving healthcare and eradicating drug trafficking, crime and terrorism. The government of Pir Sabir Shah in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was toppled and Aftab Ahmad Khan Sherpao took over as Chief Minister, and the government of Zulfiqar Ali Magsi in Balochistan was also brought down. In June 1994 her government presented a budget proposing new taxes of Rupees 128 billion, which diminished its popularity. On November 5, 1996 President Farooq Ahmad Khan Laghari, in exercise of Article 58(2)B, dissolved the National Assembly and appointed Malak Mairaj Khalid as Caretaker Prime Minister.

Q: 5. What do you know about Nawaz Sharif's first government?

Ans: Nawaz Sharif was invited by President Ghulam Ishaq Khan on November 6, 1990 to form the government. On January 27, 1991 the governments of India and Pakistan ratified the agreement not to attack each other's nuclear installations. He announced the distribution of resources between the Federation and the Provinces through the National Finance Commission Award, which gave the provinces financial independence from the centre. In 1991 the Chief Ministers of all four provinces signed an agreement on the distribution of the waters of the river Indus, the Council of Common Interests approved it, and the Indus River System Authority (IRSA) was formed to implement it. On January 22, 1991 the Privatization Commission was formed to privatize loss-making state enterprises; reforms facilitated foreign investment and exports increased up to 12 percent. An agricultural policy with financial and non-financial incentives for farmers was announced. The Shariat Bill 1991 was passed by the National Assembly to ensure the primacy of the Quran and Sunna in legal and administrative affairs, and the Bait-ul-Mal was created for the welfare of the poor and needy. A Self-Employment Scheme gave the unemployed loans of fifty thousand, one hundred and fifty thousand and three hundred thousand rupees, and a Labour Policy gave an adhoc allowance to employees of grade one to sixteen. In 1992 the Islamabad-Lahore Motorway was launched and a public transport programme for self-employed youth was initiated on September 5, 1992, with vehicles available on only 10 percent down payment. On April 18, 1993 the President dissolved the assemblies and dismissed him, but on May 26, 1993 the Supreme Court struck down the dissolution and restored his government. Finally, on July 18, 1993, Ghulam Ishaq Khan dissolved the National Assembly and resigned himself; Waseem Sajjad became Acting President and Moeen Qureshi the Caretaker Prime Minister.

Q: 6. Write a comprehensive note on the regime of General Pervez Musharraf.

Ans: On October 12, 1999 Nawaz Sharif removed General Pervez Musharraf as Chief of Army Staff, but Musharraf did not comply; his plane was not allowed to land at Karachi Airport, the army acted, and Musharraf overthrew the government and assumed the title of Chief Executive. On June 20, 2001 he removed Muhammad Rafiq Tarrar and himself became the President of Pakistan. His regime introduced the devolution of power through local governments (three-tier Union, Tehsil/Town and District Councils), with the National Reconstruction Bureau implementing the plan. A presidential referendum was held on April 30, 2002, giving him a heavy mandate for five years as President, and on August 21, 2002 he issued the Legal Framework Order (LFO), which empowered the President to amend the Constitution. General elections were held on October 10, 2002; the Pakistan Muslim League (Q) emerged as the largest party in the National Assembly with 72 seats, the Peoples' Party was second with 63 and the MMA secured 45; PML(Q) formed governments in Punjab and Sindh and the MMA in NWFP (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) and Balochistan. After the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, Pakistan cooperated with the United States in the war against terrorism. Under Musharraf and Prime Minister Shaukat Aziz, economic reforms were introduced: the General Sales Tax was implemented, the tax rate was reduced while the tax net was widened, provincial taxes were introduced and the office of the Tax Mohtasib was established; privatization of banks and industries raised about 5 percent of citizens from the poverty level to the middle class, and according to a World Bank report Pakistan witnessed 6.8 percent growth in the last eight years of the regime. The Higher Education Commission was established, and computerized National Identity Cards and a national database were introduced. A defence exhibition, Ideas 2000, was held in Karachi in November 2000. In 2007 Musharraf declared an emergency and suspended the Chief Justice, and on December 27, 2007 Benazir Bhutto was assassinated in Rawalpindi. After the elections of February 18, 2008, Yousaf Raza Gilani became Prime Minister; Musharraf resigned from the Presidency on August 18, 2008 and Asif Ali Zardari was elected President on September 6, 2008.

lessons.title: Activity
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The chapter's activities are a Pakistan History competition, a timeline of the heads of government and state from 1971 to 2008, and a quiz on the persons of the chapter.
  • The timeline runs from Bhutto's takeover on December 20, 1971 to the election of Asif Ali Zardari as President on September 6, 2008.

Solved Exercises

Activity

Q: 1. Arrange a competition on the subject of Pakistan History.

Ans: This is a classroom activity. The class is divided into teams and a Pakistan History competition is arranged on the events of this chapter: the Bhutto reforms, the 1973 Constitution, the Islamization under Zia-ul-Haq, the Junejo government and the Afghan Jihad, the governments of Benazir Bhutto and Nawaz Sharif, Pakistan becoming a nuclear power on May 28, 1998, and the Musharraf regime. Each team is asked questions in turn from the chapter, marks are awarded for correct answers, and the team with the highest score is declared the winner.

Q: 2. Draw a timeline showing the successive heads of governments and heads of state in Pakistan between 1971 and 2008.

Ans: Timeline from this chapter: December 20, 1971 - Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto takes over as the first Civilian Martial Law Administrator, later Prime Minister under the 1973 Constitution. July 5, 1977 - General Zia-ul-Haq topples Bhutto's government; September 1978 - Zia declares himself President. March 23, 1985 - Muhammad Khan Junejo takes oath as Prime Minister; May 30, 1988 - his government is dismissed. August 17, 1988 - Zia dies in the Bahawalpur plane crash; Ghulam Ishaq Khan, Chairman Senate, becomes President. lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The fundamental objectives of Pakistan's foreign policy are national integrity and security, ideological protection and economic development.
  • Pakistan lies in the north-west of South Asia, in the centre of the Muslim world; the Karakoram Highway and the ports of Karachi and Gwadar make its location important for the whole region.
  • Pak-China relations include the 1963 border treaty and first trade agreement, the Karakoram Highway, Gwadar Port and the JF-17 Thunder jets.
  • Pakistan signed an aviation treaty with Uzbekistan at Karachi in 1992 and a bilateral trade agreement in March 1992.
  • The OIC came into being after the 1969 fire in the occupied Bait-ul-Muqaddas; its headquarters is at Jeddah and it has 57 member states.
  • Pakistan has been a UN member since September 30, 1947 and contributes troops and police to UN peace-keeping missions.
  • Afghanistan was the only country that opposed Pakistan's membership of the UNO; in 1996 Pakistan was among the three countries that recognized the Taliban government.

Solved Exercises

Exercise II: Give short answers to the following questions

Q: 1. What are the fundamental objectives of Pakistan's foreign policy?

Ans: The fundamental objectives of Pakistan's foreign policy are: (1) National Integrity and Security: safeguarding and promoting national interests is the fundamental goal of Pakistan's foreign policy; as an Islamic state, Pakistan seeks to ensure the security of its borders and promote the well-being of its citizens. (2) Ideological Protection: Pakistan's ideology has its roots in Islam, so the country endeavours to protect the ideology of Islam; Muslim unity is at the centre of its foreign policy, and it plays an active role in the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) and the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO). (3) Economic Development: Pakistan wants better relations with those countries with whom trade or economic co-operation can help achieve development, and in recent years it has adopted its foreign policy keeping in view the trends of economic liberalization, free trade and privatization.

Q: 2. What is the importance of Pakistan's geographical location?

Ans: Pakistan occupies a very important geo-political location in the north-west of South Asia. It is surrounded by Afghanistan in the west, Iran in the south-west, China in the north-east, India in the east and the Arabian Sea in the south. It lies in the centre of the Muslim world, stretching from Morocco in the west to Indonesia in the east, a region rich in natural resources like oil, gas and minerals. The Karakoram Highway is an important trade route between Pakistan and China, and Karachi port is situated at the crossroads of world trade routes, both marine and aerial. The Gwadar port, built with Chinese co-operation, has increased Pakistan's strategic importance. Landlocked countries like Afghanistan and the Central Asian states can carry out international trade through Pakistan's ports, which makes Pakistan's location important for the whole region.

Q: 3. Write a note on Pak-China relations.

Ans: Pakistan recognized Communist China after the Communist Revolution and continued diplomatic relations with it. During the 1960s the relations between the two countries were very friendly, and Pakistan played a pivotal role in the restoration of China as a permanent member of the UN Security Council. The border dispute between the two countries was peacefully resolved through a treaty signed at Peking in 1963, and the first trade agreement was also signed the same year, under which China imported jute, cotton, chromite, leather and leather goods, cement, chemicals and raw material from Pakistan. The two countries have strong relations in defence production; the JF-17 Thunder fighter jets are a symbol of this co-operation. The Karakoram Highway and Gwadar Port, Pakistan's second largest port after Karachi, are monuments of Pak-China co-operation; other examples are the Heavy Mechanical Complex at Taxila, the Aeronautical Complex at Kamra, the Saindak Project, the Chashma Power Plant, the Chitral Tunnel and the Al-Khalid Tanks. The two countries also have similar positions on many issues at the United Nations.

Q: 4. Write a note on Pak-Uzbekistan relations.

Ans: After the disintegration of the Soviet Union, Pakistan recognized Uzbekistan and established diplomatic relations with it. In 1992 an aviation treaty was signed between the two countries at Karachi, and in March 1992 they entered into a bilateral agreement promoting economic and trade relations between the private sectors of both countries. Co-operation has since expanded in the fields of energy, trade, banking and communications. Uzbekistan holds the view that the Kashmir issue should be settled amicably in accordance with the wishes of the people of Kashmir, who are the main stakeholders in the issue. Frequent meetings at the summit level have helped improve relations between the two countries.

Q: 5. What is OIC? Why did it come into being?

Ans: OIC stands for the Organization of Islamic Cooperation. It came into being after an incident of fire in the occupied Bait-ul-Muqaddas in 1969: the foreign ministers of the Arab countries proposed that a summit conference of the Muslim countries be held, and the task of organizing it was assigned to the foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia and Morocco. A seven-member committee consisting of Morocco, Saudi Arabia, Iran, Malaysia, Nigeria, Pakistan and Somalia was formed, and the conference was held at Rabat in September 1969, in which twenty-four Muslim countries participated; this led to the creation of the OIC. Its objectives include resolving the problems faced by the Muslim world, supporting the Palestinian liberation movement, ensuring the defence of Muslim holy places, and defending the independence and territorial integrity of member states. Its summit is held every three years, its headquarters is at Jeddah, and at present it has 57 member states, making it the largest organization of the Islamic world.

Q: 6. Write a note on Pakistan's role in the UN.

Ans: Pakistan has been a member of the United Nations Organization since September 30, 1947 and plays an active role in it. On several occasions Pakistan has been elected a non-permanent member of the Security Council. Pakistan offers the services of its military and police forces to the peace-keeping missions of the United Nations, which operate all over the world. Several UN agencies, including the UNDP, WFP, WHO, UNICEF, UNESCO, IFAD, UNHCR and UN Habitat, render humanitarian assistance, social welfare and economic development services in Pakistan. However, the UN has disappointed Pakistan in the resolution of the Kashmir issue, which remains unresolved since 1948 despite the Security Council resolutions of August 13, 1948 and January 5, 1949 calling for a plebiscite.

Q: 7. Write a note on Pak-Afghanistan relations.

Ans: Afghanistan and Pakistan have deep religious, historical and cultural ties, yet their relations have not been very friendly. Afghanistan was the only country that opposed Pakistan's membership of the UNO, but the UNO admitted Pakistan on September 30, 1947. The Prime Minister of Pakistan visited Afghanistan in August 1956 and the Afghan Prime Minister visited Pakistan in November 1956, and in 1958 Pakistan agreed to Afghan transit trade. After the communist revolution in Afghanistan, Pakistan supported the armed resistance, out of Islamic spirit and national interest, and sheltered millions of Afghan refugees. In 1992 Pakistan recognized the Mujahideen government in Kabul, and in 1996, when the Taliban took over Kabul, Pakistan was among the three countries that recognized the Taliban government. After the United States and NATO invaded Afghanistan following the attacks of September 11, 2001, the Taliban government was toppled; Pakistan recognized the democratic government of Hamid Karzai and is among the prominent countries providing financial assistance to Afghanistan.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Friendly relations with neighbours protect Pakistan's borders and open trade routes for the landlocked states through its ports.
  • Iran was the first country to recognize Pakistan; the RCD pact was signed in 1964 and the ECO succeeded it in 1985; Iran supported Pakistan in the wars of 1965 and 1971.
  • Pakistan signed a mutual defence pact with the USA in May 1954 and joined CENTO and SEATO, which it later left.
  • Britain wrote off 64 million pounds of Pakistan's debt in 1979; the European Union receives 20 percent of Pakistan's exports.
  • Pakistan established diplomatic relations with Japan in 1952 and exports cotton to Japan.
  • Kashmir had a 75 percent Muslim population; the Maharaja signed the Standstill Agreement with Pakistan on August 12, 1947 and proclaimed accession to India on October 27, 1947.
  • The UN resolutions of August 13, 1948 and January 5, 1949 called for a plebiscite in Kashmir, which has never been held; the Agra meeting was held in July 2001.

Solved Exercises

Exercise III: Give detailed answers to the following questions

Q: 1. What is the importance of Pakistan's relations with its neighboring countries?

Ans: Relations with neighbouring countries are of special importance for Pakistan because its security, trade and ideology are directly linked with them. With China, Pakistan has very friendly relations: the border treaty and first trade agreement of 1963, the Karakoram Highway, Gwadar Port, the JF-17 Thunder jets and projects like the Heavy Mechanical Complex Taxila, Saindak and Chashma are monuments of this co-operation. With India, relations have remained strained since independence, the fundamental cause being the Kashmir dispute, over which three wars have been fought; the Indus Basin Water Treaty of 1960 settled the water dispute, the Simla Agreement of July 1972 provided for resolving disputes through bilateral dialogue, and in 1988 the two countries agreed not to attack each other's nuclear installations, yet tension persists. Iran was the first country to recognize Pakistan; the Shah of Iran visited Pakistan in 1950, the RCD pact was signed in 1964, and Iran supported Pakistan in the wars of 1965 and 1971; after the Islamic Revolution of 1979 the RCD was succeeded by the ECO in 1985. With Afghanistan, despite deep religious and cultural ties, relations have often been uneasy: Afghanistan opposed Pakistan's UN membership, but Pakistan sheltered millions of Afghan refugees after the communist revolution and continues to assist Afghanistan. Friendly relations with neighbours protect Pakistan's borders, open trade routes for the landlocked states through its ports and strengthen the unity of the Muslim world.

Q: 2. Write a note on Pakistan's relations with the Central Asian Republics.

Ans: After the disintegration of the Soviet Union, Pakistan recognized the Central Asian Republics - Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan - and established diplomatic relations with them. With Uzbekistan, an aviation treaty was signed at Karachi in 1992 and a bilateral agreement in March 1992 promoted private-sector economic and trade relations; co-operation covers energy, trade, banking and communications, and Uzbekistan supports an amicable settlement of Kashmir according to the wishes of the Kashmiri people. With Turkmenistan, with which Pakistan shares religion, culture and history, the PIA and the National Bank of Pakistan opened offices in Ashkabad; an agreement to purchase natural gas was signed in 1991 and a joint commission for co-operation was established in 1999. Kazakhstan is the largest country of the Muslim world in terms of territory; during the Kazakh President's visit in 1992 agreements on science and technology, trade, economy and communications were signed, and in 1998 a Transit Trade agreement was signed by Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and China. With Kyrgyzstan, agreements on economic and cultural ties (1991) and on controlling drug trafficking were signed; in 1994 the four countries agreed to upgrade the Karakoram Highway to international standards and extend it to Almatay and Bishkek, and diplomatic missions were first exchanged in 1994. Tajikistan is Pakistan's closest Central Asian neighbour, separated by the narrow Wakhan belt; in January 1992 it offered to supply electric power to Pakistan, air-transport agreements were signed, Pakistan offered it transit trade facilities, and in 1994 agreements on science and technology, trade and economic affairs were concluded.

Q: 3. What is the importance of Pakistan's relations with Saudi Arabia?

Ans: Pakistan's relations with Saudi Arabia are time-tested and of great importance. The Kingdom supported the Pakistan Movement even before the creation of Pakistan and was among the countries that recognized Pakistan at the earliest. Saudi Arabia has provided Pakistan diplomatic, moral and economic support at every difficult time, and these relations grew dramatically during Zia's regime. Tens of thousands of Pakistanis are employed in Saudi Arabia and send huge amounts of foreign exchange home, which contributes significantly to Pakistan's economy. The Faisal Mosque and the International Islamic University in Islamabad were built with Saudi financial support. After Pakistan's nuclear tests of May 1998, when economic sanctions were imposed, Saudi Arabia provided oil on soft loans, and it also gave ample assistance after the devastating earthquake of October 8, 2005. Thus Saudi Arabia is important for Pakistan religiously, economically and diplomatically.

Q: 4. Analyze Pakistan's relations with the Big Powers.

Ans: Pakistan has always sought friendly relations with the big powers - the USA, China, Britain, Russia, the European Union and Japan - for its economic and military growth. With the United States, relations have seen many ups and downs: Pakistan formally joined the CENTO and SEATO alliances and signed a mutual defence pact in May 1954, but in the 1965 war the US gave no help and imposed an arms embargo, and in 1971 it gave no substantial support, after which Pakistan left SEATO and CENTO and tilted towards non-alignment. In 1979 the two countries collaborated in supporting the Afghans against the Soviet-backed Kabul government, but after the Soviet withdrawal in 1989 American interest waned, and in 1998 the US imposed economic sanctions on both India and Pakistan after the nuclear tests; after September 2001 the alliance was renewed in the war against terrorism. With Britain, relations are important because of the Commonwealth: Britain was among the first to recognize Pakistan, the Rann of Kutch issue was resolved through Britain's efforts in 1965, Britain wrote off 64 million pounds of Pakistan's debt in 1979, and Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher visited in 1981 and announced aid for the Afghan refugees. The European Union receives 20 percent of Pakistan's exports and is among the largest donors of aid in health, education, population welfare, human development, environmental protection and the eradication of child labour and drug abuse; relations grew particularly after the EU-Pakistan summit of 2009. Japan established diplomatic relations with Pakistan in 1952; Pakistan exports cotton to Japan, and Japan has helped Pakistan's industrial growth with massive financial aid and investment, seen in projects like the Indus Highway, the Kohat Tunnel, PIMS Islamabad and the Ghazi Brotha Power Project. Relations with Russia began in 1948, were warm during 1947-1950, cooled in 1958, reached their lowest in the 1980s because of Pakistan's support to the Afghan Mujahideen, and have been improving since the new millennium. The lesson of these relations is that in international affairs there are no permanent friends or foes; only national interests are permanent.

Q: 5. Write about the Kashmir issue and Pak-India relations in detail.

Ans: The Kashmir issue goes back to the Partition of the Subcontinent. Under the Plan of June 3, 1947, the rulers of the princely states were free to join either India or Pakistan, keeping in view the wishes of their population and the geographical location of their states. Kashmir was ruled by a Hindu Maharaja, Hari Singh Dogra; on August 12, 1947 a Standstill Agreement was signed between the Maharaja and Pakistan so that no hasty decision was taken. But on October 27, 1947, despite Kashmir's proximity to Pakistan and its 75 percent Muslim population, the Maharaja proclaimed accession to India and requested Indian military assistance. The people of Kashmir rose in armed revolt, and in 1947-48 Pakistan supported their liberation movement; the areas adjoining Pakistan were liberated and the Azad Kashmir government was established. On January 1, 1948 India took the matter to the UN Security Council; the UN enforced a ceasefire and passed resolutions on August 13, 1948 and January 5, 1949 calling for a plebiscite under UN mandate on the principle of self-determination, but these resolutions were never implemented and India has squarely refused to hold the plebiscite. Pakistan maintains its principled moral and diplomatic support to the freedom fighters. Because of Kashmir, Pakistan-India relations have remained strained since independence and three wars have been fought. The water dispute was resolved through the Indus Basin Treaty of 1960 with the help of the World Bank. In 1971 India supported the secessionists, which led to the Fall of Dacca. The Simla Agreement of July 1972 provided for resolving disputes through bilateral dialogue; in 1988 the two prime ministers signed an agreement barring attacks on each other's nuclear installations at the SAARC conference, and in 1989 the armed struggle in Indian-held Kashmir gathered momentum. India wants the issue resolved bilaterally without a third party, while Pakistan wants it resolved in accordance with the UN resolutions. The Agra meeting of July 14-17, 2001 ended without conclusion, but in 2004 the two countries agreed at the SAARC meeting in Islamabad and at the UN General Assembly to continue the dialogue.

Key Points

  • The chapter's activities are pointing out the Muslim world and SAARC countries on a world map, a debate on Pakistan's role in the UN, and a list of the organizations joined by Pakistan.
  • The organizations listed are the UNO (1947), the Commonwealth, SEATO and CENTO, the RCD (1964), the OIC (1969), the ECO (1985), SAARC and the D-8 (1997).

Solved Exercises

Activity

Q: 1. Point out the Muslim world and SAARC countries on a world map.

Ans: This is a classroom activity. On a world map, the students point out the Muslim world - the countries named in this chapter: Afghanistan, Iran, Indonesia, Jordan, Bangladesh, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Palestine, Libya, the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, Syria, Iraq, Kuwait, Malaysia and the Central Asian Muslim states - and the SAARC countries: Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, the Maldives and Bhutan, with Afghanistan, which joined SAARC in recent years. The exercise shows that Pakistan lies in the centre of the Muslim world, stretching from Morocco in the west to Indonesia in the east.

Q: 2. Arrange a debate on Pakistan's Role in the UN.

Ans: This is a classroom activity. A debate is arranged on the subject 'Pakistan's Role in the UN'. Speaking points from this chapter: Pakistan has been a member of the UNO since September 30, 1947 and plays an active role in it; it has been elected a non-permanent member of the Security Council on several occasions; it offers the services of its military and police forces to UN peace-keeping missions all over the world; and UN agencies such as UNDP, WFP, WHO, UNICEF, UNESCO, IFAD, UNHCR and UN Habitat serve in Pakistan in humanitarian assistance, social welfare and economic development. The other side may note that the UN has disappointed Pakistan on the Kashmir issue, which remains unresolved since 1948 despite the plebiscite resolutions of 1948 and 1949.

Q: 3. Prepare a list of all the regional and international organizations and alliances joined by Pakistan since her inception.

Ans: The regional and international organizations and alliances joined by Pakistan since her inception, as given in this chapter, are: (1) the United Nations Organization (UNO), joined on September 30, 1947; (2) the Commonwealth, through which Pakistan's relations with Britain carry special importance; (3) SEATO and CENTO, the defence alliances Pakistan formally joined in the 1950s (a mutual defence pact with the USA was signed in May 1954), which Pakistan later left; (4) the RCD (Regional Co-operation for Development), formed in 1964 by Pakistan, Iran and Turkey, which became defunct after the Islamic Revolution in Iran in 1979; (5) the OIC (Organization of Islamic Cooperation), created at Rabat in September 1969, with headquarters at Jeddah and 57 member states at present; (6) the ECO (Economic Cooperation Organization), founded in 1985 as the successor of the RCD to promote mutual economic co-operation, later joined by Afghanistan and the Central Asian republics; (7) SAARC (South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation), whose first summit was held in 1985 at Dacca, with its head office at Kathmandu; and (8) the D-8, formed in 1997 by Pakistan, Iran and six other developing countries.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Crude oil is the most important source of energy for Pakistan; only about ten percent of demand is met from domestic production and about ninety percent is imported.
  • Natural gas is used in households, cars, fertilizer and cement factories and thermal power houses; most of Pakistan's gas comes from Sui, where it was first discovered during 1950-52 at a depth of about 4,000 feet.
  • The Thar coal deposits, estimated at about 175 billion tons, are the world's largest coal reserve, though most Pakistani coal is low grade.
  • Agriculture is the backbone of the economy: 65 percent of the population is linked with it; chemical fertilizer use rose from 1,000 tons in 1952-53 to 2.4 million tons in 2002-03.
  • About seventy percent of the cultivated area is irrigated by canals and about thirty percent by tube-wells; the Karez method is used in Balochistan.
  • Cottage and small scale industries employ about eighty percent of the industrial labour force but contribute only about 2.5 percent of the GDP.
  • Pakistan's major sea ports are Karachi, Muhammad Bin Qasim Port (about 35 kilometers from Karachi) and Gwadar; the Lahore Dry Port was built in 1974.

Solved Exercises

Exercise II: Write short answers to the following questions

Q: 1. Write a note on Mineral Oil (Crude Oil).

Ans: Mineral oil, or crude oil (petroleum), is the most important source of energy for Pakistan. Unfortunately only about ten percent of the country's demand for crude oil is met from domestic production, while about ninety percent has to be imported at a huge cost in foreign exchange, which is a major source of Pakistan's trade deficit. Crude oil reserves in Pakistan are located at Kot Sarang, Toot, Mial, Khor and Dhallan in the Attock region, Dhoduk in Dera Ghazi Khan, Karsal in Jehlum, in District Badin in Sindh and at Adhi Qazian in Rawalpindi. Important reserves have also been discovered in southern Sindh.

Q: 2. Write notes on: i. Natural Gas, ii. Coal, iii. Agriculture.

Ans: i. Natural Gas: Natural gas is used in households, in cars, in fertilizer factories, in cement factories and in thermal power houses. Twenty-nine percent of it is used in the fertilizer factories and 24 percent in other factories. Its reserves are found at Sui in Balochistan; at Khairpur, Sari, Hundi, Mazrani, Kandkot and Saring in Sindh; at Dhoduk, Pirkoh, Dhalian and Mial in Punjab; and at Gurguri near Karak in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Gas was first discovered at Sui in Balochistan during 1950-52, while digging for crude oil, at a depth of about 4,000 feet, and most of Pakistan's gas comes from Sui. ii. Coal: Coal reserves in Pakistan are found at Mach, Khosat, Harnai, Sinjidi, Pir Ismail Ziarat and Sor-Range Degari in Balochistan, at Lakhra in Dadu, Makerwal in Mianwali, Jhinmpur in Thatta and at Thar in Tharparker. The world's largest coal reserve has been discovered at Thar, estimated at about 175 billion tons, but it has not yet been properly exploited. Most of Pakistan's coal is not of a high grade; it is used largely in brick manufacturing and in the cement industries. iii. Agriculture: Agriculture is the backbone of Pakistan's economy. Sixty-five percent of the population is directly or indirectly linked with this sector; it provides raw material for most of the industries and contributes about 32 percent of the GDP and about 45 percent of the foreign exchange earnings. The use of chemical fertilizer rose from 1,000 tons in 1952-53 to 2.4 million tons in 2002-03, and agricultural universities at Peshawar, Faisalabad, Rawalpindi and Tandojam are working for its development.

Q: 3. Describe briefly the sources of irrigation in Pakistan.

Ans: The sources of irrigation in Pakistan are briefly as follows. (1) Canals: Pakistan's canal system is among the most important in the world; a network of dams, barrages, head-works and canals exists in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab and Sindh, and about seventy percent of the total cultivated area is irrigated by canals. Barrages have been built on the river Indus at Chashma, Kalabagh, Taunsa, Gaddu and Kotri, and also on the Jhelum and the Chenab. (2) Tube-wells: tens of thousands of tube-wells irrigate about thirty percent of the land; the government encourages solar systems for running tube-wells. (3) Wells: where the water level is high, water is still drawn from wells by animal power. (4) Karez: in Balochistan, ground water is drawn through underground canals from elevated ground to the lower plains; this method is falling into disuse as ground water dwindles. (5) Dams: the three largest dams, Tarbela, Mangla and Warsak, store water for irrigation and also generate electricity.

Q: 4. Which industries are included in the cottage and small scale industries?

Ans: Cottage and small scale industries rely more on human labour than on machines. They play an important role in meeting local and domestic needs and also earn foreign exchange through exports. The industries included in them are: the carpet industry, metalwork, hosiery, shoes, sports goods, surgical instruments, plastic goods, carpentry and leather goods. About eighty percent of the industrial labour force is employed in the cottage and small scale industries, although their contribution to the GDP is only about 2.5 percent.

Q: 5. What is meant by imports? What are Pakistan's major imports?

Ans: Imports mean the goods and commodities that a country purchases from other countries. Pakistan's major imports are: automobile and automobile parts, chemicals, fertilizer, medicines, machinery, iron, petroleum, industrial raw material, stationery, cooking oil, tea, weapons and defense technology. Pakistan imports these goods mainly from China, Japan, the United States, Kuwait, the United Kingdom, the European Union, Saudi Arabia, Malaysia and various Asian and African countries.

Q: 6. What is meant by exports? What are Pakistan's major exports?

Ans: Exports mean the goods and commodities that a country sells to other countries. Pakistan's major exports are: cotton, cloth, garments, woolen products, rugs, leather goods, sports goods, surgical implements, fish, rice, vegetables and fruits. Pakistan exports these goods mainly to Saudi Arabia, Dubai, the European Union, the United Kingdom, the United States, Japan, Hong Kong and various Asian and African countries. In the beginning Pakistan exported only agricultural products, but now the share of industrial goods in its exports keeps increasing.

Q: 7. Write a note on Pakistan's major sea ports.

Ans: Pakistan's major sea ports are: (1) Karachi Port, the oldest port of Pakistan, situated on the Arabian Sea, the northern part of the Indian Ocean, which has been a lifeline of international trade since the middle ages; it is among the important ports of the region and can serve as a gateway for Afghanistan and the Central Asian Republics. (2) Muhammad Bin Qasim Port, built some 35 kilometers from Karachi in view of the Pakistan Steel Mills and the country's growing international trade. (3) Gwadar Port in Balochistan, built with Chinese co-operation, which is expected to assume an ever-greater role in trade and development. There are also small ports at Ormara, Pasni and Jeevani, which are basically large fish markets. In addition, dry ports have been set up inland, the most important being the Lahore Dry Port built in 1974 at the railways depot, with others at Rawalpindi, Peshawar, Sialkot, Faisalabad, Multan, Quetta and Haiderabad.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Pakistan's mineral resources include crude oil, natural gas, coal, iron, chromite, copper, carbonate, marble, gypsum, sulphur, china clay and salt, though they are extremely underutilized.
  • High-grade iron ore is found at Nokandi in Balochistan, chromite at Muslim Bagh, Chaghi and Kharan, and vast copper deposits have been discovered at Recodik.
  • The causes of low agricultural production include traditional farming methods, lack of finance, continual division of land, crop diseases, and water-logging and salinity.
  • Wheat is the staple food crop; about 75 percent of tobacco is produced in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and 25 percent in Punjab.
  • Industries add value to raw material, raise the GDP and create employment; the Pakistan Industrial Development Corporation was established in 1952.
  • Natural gas, petroleum, coal and hydroelectric power meet about 65 percent of energy needs; about 70 percent of electricity is thermal.
  • The Karachi nuclear power station has a capacity of 137 megawatts and the Chashma plant 300 megawatts; water, wind and sun are renewable sources of energy.

Solved Exercises

Exercise III: Give comprehensive answers to the following questions

Q: 1. Write a note on the mineral resources of Pakistan.

Ans: Pakistan is rich in mineral resources, which include crude oil, natural gas, coal, iron, chromite, copper, carbonate, marble, gypsum, sulphur, china clay and salt, though these reserves are extremely underutilized. (1) Crude Oil: the most important energy source; only about ten percent of demand is met locally and about ninety percent is imported. Reserves are found at Kot Sarang, Toot, Mial, Khor and Dhallan (Attock), Dhoduk (Dera Ghazi Khan), Karsal (Jehlum), Badin and Adhi Qazian (Rawalpindi), with important reserves in southern Sindh. (2) Natural Gas: used in households, transport and industries; 29 percent goes to fertilizer factories and 24 percent to other factories. Reserves are at Sui (Balochistan), Khairpur, Sari, Hundi, Mazrani, Kandkot and Saring (Sindh), Dhoduk, Pirkoh, Dhalian and Mial (Punjab) and Gurguri near Karak (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa). (3) Coal: found at Mach, Khosat, Harnai, Sinjidi, Pir Ismail Ziarat and Sor-Range Degari (Balochistan), Lakhra, Makerwal, Jhinmpur and Thar; the Thar deposits, estimated at 175 billion tons, are the world's largest coal reserve, though most Pakistani coal is low grade and is used in brick and cement industries. (4) Crude Iron: low-grade ores at Chalghazi, Kalabagh, Langrial and Chitral, and high-grade ore at Nokandi in Balochistan. (5) Gypsum: at Daudkhel, Khewra and Dandot, used in the fertilizer and cement industries and for plaster of Paris. (6) Marble: high-grade marble of many colours - white, green, brown and ash - in Swat, Mardan, Nowshera and Malagori near Warsak, Chinai (Balochistan) and the Mohmand and Bajaur Agencies; it is an important export. (7) Carbonate: used in construction and the cement and glass industries, found at Kohat, Margalla, Taxila, Ranipur, Harnai and Rohri. (8) Chromite: abundant, used in the iron and paint industries and photographic materials, found at Muslim Bagh, Chaghi and Kharan (Balochistan), Charsadda and Malakand (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) and North Waziristan. (9) Salt: vast deposits at Khewra, Bahadur Khel and Jatta, and also obtained from sea-water on the Balochistan coast. (10) Sulphur: used in chemical industries such as explosives; vast deposits in Balochistan, and also at Mardan and Jacobabad, with extraction factories at Quetta and Karachi. (11) Copper: at Saindak and Chaghi in Balochistan, with vast deposits recently discovered at Recodik; it is used for electrical wire, household utensils and minting coins.

Q: 2. What are the causes of low agricultural production in Pakistan and what steps are being taken to promote production in the agricultural sector?

Ans: The causes of low agricultural production in Pakistan are: (1) Traditional farming methods: most farmers still use traditional methods, so the per-acre yield is low. (2) Lack of financial resources: poor farmers cannot afford fertilizer, seed and modern technology. (3) Continual division of land: through inheritance, holdings keep dividing into pieces too small for mechanization. (4) Shortage of cultivated land: with population growth, agricultural land is converted to residential areas. (5) Crop diseases: plant diseases and pests reduce production, and pesticides are costly. (6) Water-logging and salinity: every year more land is rendered uncultivable. (7) Lack of education in agricultural sciences among farmers. (8) Shortage of water for irrigation. (9) Lack of agricultural research, as there are too few institutions and resources. The steps being taken to promote production are: (1) salinity control programmes and reclamation of land; (2) ending absentee landlordism so that hundreds of thousands of uncultivated acres are brought under cultivation; (3) land reforms to motivate farmers; (4) agricultural education and research; (5) chemical fertilizers, made available in time at lower cost under price control; (6) better irrigation through new tube-wells and small dams; (7) provision of loan facilities on a more energetic and flexible basis; (8) provision of modern agricultural machinery and mechanization; and (9) flood control through new dams, which also store water for dry-season irrigation.

Q: 3. Which crops are grown in Pakistan? Describe in detail.

Ans: The major crops grown in Pakistan are: (1) Wheat: the most important crop and the staple food of the people; it is grown throughout the country, mostly in the irrigated plains and on a small scale in the barani (arid) areas; the Potohar region is also a wheat-growing area. (2) Rice: a main food crop; Pakistan is self-sufficient in rice and an important exporter of high-quality rice; it is grown in the warm plains of Punjab and Sindh and also in the mountainous regions of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the Northern Areas. (3) Cotton: an important crop and a huge source of foreign exchange, grown in the southern plains of Punjab and Sindh. (4) Sugarcane: grown in the warmer climates of Punjab, Sindh and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa where enough irrigation water is available. (5) Maize: a staple food in many rural areas; its non-edible parts are fed to livestock and it is also used for obtaining edible oil; it is grown in most regions of Pakistan and Azad Kashmir. (6) Tobacco: among the most important cash crops; about 75 percent is produced in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and 25 percent in Punjab. (7) Pulses: Chana (Gram), Massoor (red Lentil), Mong (Green gram) and Mash (Yellow Lentil), grown in the barani areas of Punjab, Sindh and the southern districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Q: 4. Describe the role of industries in national economic development and give an account of the country's small and large industries.

Ans: Industries play a vital role in national economic development. They add value to raw material - for example, cotton is turned into cloth - which generates capital and increases national wealth. They raise the Gross Domestic Product (GDP), create employment for the people, and form the base of a nation's economic power, on which its political and military power also depends. To develop industry the government established the Pakistan Industrial Board (1948), the Pakistan Industrial Investment Corporation (1949), the Pakistan Industrial Development Corporation (1952) and the Pakistan Industries Development Bank. Cottage and small scale industries rely more on human labour than on machines; they include the carpet industry, metalwork, hosiery, shoes, sports goods, surgical instruments, plastic goods, carpentry and leather goods. About eighty percent of the industrial labour force is employed in them, though their contribution to the GDP is only about 2.5 percent; they meet local needs and earn foreign exchange through exports. Large industries require large amounts of finance and infrastructure such as communications, power, water, telecommunications, raw materials and trained labour, and the government has established big industrial zones for them. They include the textile, sugar, edible oil, fertilizer, cement, leather shoes, iron and steel, heavy machinery, chemical, oil refinery and petroleum industries. Today Pakistan manufactures and exports textiles, woollen cloth, vegetable oil, match-boxes, leather goods, rubber, cement, cigarettes and sugar, in which it is self-sufficient and an exporter.

Q: 5. What is meant by sources of energy? Describe the different sources of energy.

Ans: Sources of energy are the means through which energy is obtained for running homes, transport, factories and power houses. Natural gas, petroleum, coal and hydroelectric power meet about 65 percent of Pakistan's energy needs, while the remaining 35 percent comes from the traditional burning of wood and biomass. The different sources are: (1) Natural Gas: first discovered at Sui in Balochistan during 1950-52 while digging for crude oil, about 4,000 feet below the surface; most of Pakistan's gas comes from Sui and it is used in households, transportation and industries, especially fertilizers and thermal power stations. (2) Petroleum (Crude Oil): domestic production is insufficient and about ninety percent is imported; reserves exist at Attock, Rawalpindi, Jehlum, Dera Ghazi Khan and Badin, and refineries operate at Karachi, Hub, Multan, Rawalpindi and Attock. (3) Coal: found in Balochistan, Sindh and Punjab, with the huge Thar deposits; it is largely low grade and used in brick and cement industries. (4) Hydroelectric Power: about 30 percent of electricity is hydro-generated at Tarbela, Mangla, Warsak, Dargai and Ghazi Barotha; its installation is costly but generation is cheap and pollution-free, while about 70 percent of electricity is thermal, produced by burning gas, coal or petroleum. (5) Solar Energy: a renewable source; solar plants concentrate sunlight to boil water and drive turbines, and a small solar power station is operating in Okara, though the technology is very expensive. (6) Nuclear Energy: a 137-megawatt nuclear power station works at Karachi and the Chashma plant in Mianwali has a capacity of 300 megawatts, with another under construction; the Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission is the prime institution in this field. Gas, crude oil, coal and uranium are non-renewable sources, while water, wind and sun are renewable and inexhaustible.

Key Points

  • The population of Pakistan in 1947 was 33 million; 63.66 percent of the population is rural and 36.33 percent lives in cities.
  • Punjab is known as the land of the five rivers.
  • Ameer Crore was a Pashto poet, and the word Urdu comes from the Turkish language.
  • Mirza Qaleech Baig laid the foundations of the art of the novel in the Sindhi language.

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • About 63.66 percent of Pakistan's population lives in rural areas and 36.33 percent in urban areas; in 1947 only 15.4 percent was urban.
  • By sex, the population consists of 49 percent males and 51 percent females; about 43 percent are up to 14 years of age.
  • Punjabi culture features the Luddi dance, horse riding, devotion to Sufi saints and folk tales like Heer Ranjha, Sohni Mahiwal and Mirza Saheban.
  • Sindhi culture features the game of Malakhra, bull-racing, the Sindhi topi and ajrak, and the jirga system.
  • The city of Gujarat is famous for paintings on earthenware, and Peshawar's craftsmen are masters of engraving on bronze, copper and tin.
  • The word Urdu is of Turkish origin and means 'army'; Urdu is the national language and a symbol of national identity.
  • According to the 2013 statistics in the chapter, there are 1,127 patients for every doctor and one hospital bed for 1,786 persons; the infant mortality rate is 83 per thousand.

Solved Exercises

Exercise II: Write short answers to the following questions

Q: 1. What is the ratio of urban and rural populations in Pakistan?

Ans: According to this chapter, about 63.66 percent of Pakistan's population lives in the rural areas, while 36.33 percent lives in the urban areas. In 1947, at the time of independence, only about 15.4 percent of the population was urban and 84.6 percent was rural, which shows that large-scale migration from the villages to the cities has taken place since then.

Q: 2. Describe the age and sex composition of Pakistan's population.

Ans: By sex, the overall population of Pakistan consists of 49 percent males and 51 percent females. By age, the composition is: among men, 43.1 percent are up to 14 years of age, 53.3 percent are between 15 and 64 years, and 3.6 percent are 65 years and above; among women, 43.2 percent are up to 14 years, 53.6 percent are between 15 and 64 years, and 3.2 percent are 65 years and above. Thus the largest share of the population consists of children and young people.

Q: 3. Write a note on Punjabi culture.

Ans: Punjab is known as the land of the five rivers and is among the most fertile regions of the Indo-Pak subcontinent. Punjabi is the most widely spoken language of the province, followed by Seraiki. The salient features of Punjabi culture include the Luddi dance, horse riding, a passion for food, devotion to the Sufi saints and a love for folk literature and story telling. Its famous folk tales are Heer Ranjha, Sohni Mahiwal and Mirza Saheban.

Q: 4. What do you know about Sindhi culture?

Ans: Sindh is among the oldest inhabited regions of the world. Sindhi is the native and most widely spoken language of the province, and agriculture and fishing are the two most important traditional professions of its people. The features of Sindhi culture include the game of Malakhra, bull-racing, the embroidery patterns on women's garments, the kalah and lungi worn by men, the custom of keeping a long moustache, the famous Sindhi topi (cap) and ajrak, the popularity of bangles among women, hospitality and the jirga system.

Q: 5. What do you know about the arts and crafts of Pakistan?

Ans: The arts and crafts of Pakistan are thousands of years old. Metal crafting into jewellery, utensils and instruments predates even the Iron Age in this region; the peoples of the Indus Valley and Gandhara civilizations were experts in melting and casting bronze, carving stone into sculptures and making seals. The buildings in Lahore, Multan, Uch Shareef and Thatta are monuments of splendid Islamic architecture, and the Muslims also promoted the minting of coins, calligraphy, drawing and jewellery-making with precious stones. The jewellery and seals preserved in the museums at Peshawar, Lahore, Taxila, Hyderabad and Karachi reflect this ancient civilization. In handicrafts, the city of Gujarat is famous for paintings on earthenware; the craftsmen of Peshawar retain mastery of engraving on bronze, copper and tin implements; the goldsmiths of Peshawar, Multan, Bahawalpur and Hyderabad are renowned for their work in gold and silver; and Balochistan and Punjab are famous for hand-woven carpets, besides a rich tradition of embroidery and decoration of fabrics.

Q: 6. Write a note on Urdu language.

Ans: The word Urdu is of Turkish origin and means 'army'. The language developed under Muslim rule in the sub-continent, when speakers of various dialects interacted with one another; its vocabulary is heavily borrowed from Arabic, Persian, Turkish and the regional languages. Urdu is the national language of Pakistan and is spoken in all four provinces. It is a highly flexible language which embraces words of the regional languages and deeply influences them. It played a vital role in reflecting the Islamic traditions of the Muslims of the sub-continent and in spearheading the Pakistan Movement. Institutions like the Anjuman-e-Taraqi-e-Urdu, the Urdu Science Board and the National Language Promotion Department promote it by writing and translating foreign books on science, history, economics, international relations and arts. Besides being a link language, Urdu is a symbol of national identity.

Q: 7. How is population growth affecting the state of health services in the country?

Ans: Pakistan's health facilities are very few compared to its rapidly growing population. According to the 2013 statistics quoted in this chapter, there are 1,127 patients for every doctor, 2,245 patients for every nurse and only one hospital bed for 1,786 persons, which is very low by international standards. The infant mortality rate is 83 per thousand and the maternal mortality rate is 350 per hundred thousand, while the average life expectancy is 64 years. Private hospitals and clinics exist, but their high costs put them beyond the reach of ordinary people. As the population grows at about 1.9 percent per year, the pressure on hospitals, doctors and medicines keeps increasing, and many people die for lack of access to health services.
