lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The social problems of Pakistan include illiteracy, poverty, insufficient health facilities, social stratification, feudalism, dowry, drug trafficking, terrorism and child labour.
  • The literacy rate was 45 percent in the 1998 census and about 57.7 percent by now.
  • Islam is the dominant feature of Pakistani culture, and the culture is a mixed culture formed by Aryans, Iranians, Afghans, Greeks, Arabs, Mongolians and Turks.
  • Pakistan's population was 33 million in 1951, 130.6 million in 1998 and over 170 million in 2010; in 2004 Pakistan was the sixth largest country by population.
  • The annual growth rate has decreased from about 3.1 percent in 1981 to around 1.9 percent.
  • Waris Shah composed Heer Ranjha; Mirza Qaleech Baig introduced the modern novel into Sindhi; Khwaja Farid was a famous Seraiki poet; the Holy Quran has been translated into Brahui.
  • The Shandur Polo Festival is held at Chitral, and the Jahez Ordinance was promulgated to overcome the menace of dowry.

Solved Exercises

Exercise III: Give detailed answers to the following questions

Q: 1. Write in detail about the social problems of Pakistan.

Ans: The social problems of Pakistan, as described in this chapter, are: (1) Illiteracy: among the biggest problems of the country; education is the fundamental right of every Pakistani, yet the majority of the people are illiterate, the literacy rate being 45 percent in the 1998 census and about 57.7 percent by now, lower than India, China and Sri Lanka. (2) Poverty: the root cause of evils in society; resources are either scarce or not properly utilized. (3) Health Facilities: the health services sector is insufficient and people die for lack of access to hospitals, doctors and medicine. (4) Social Stratification: society is divided into strata on the basis of creed and caste, and the uneven distribution of wealth has created a huge gap between the rich and the poor. (5) Feudalism: most of the land and property is owned by feudal lords and the poor farmers are deprived of its benefits. (6) The Curse of Dowry: dowry has brought untold miseries for the poorer families. (7) Drug Trafficking and Smuggling: these play a big role in the destruction of society. (8) Terrorism: it has wreaked havoc, and no one feels safe or contented. (9) Child Labour: children are subjected to labour instead of receiving education; it is not just a problem but an evil.

Q: 2. What are the basic features of Pakistani culture?

Ans: Culture means all the learning, belief, art, morality and law of a society; it is a societal heritage that transmits the collective experiences of a community from generation to generation. The basic features of Pakistani culture are: (1) Islam is the dominant feature of Pakistani culture; it is against divisions on ethnic, linguistic or traditional grounds and provides a common framework that unites its followers in a single nationhood beyond territorial frontiers, while the Constitution also provides freedom and benefits to everyone. (2) Mixed culture: this region has been a melting pot since prehistory; the earliest settlers mingled with the Aryan invaders, and later Iranians, Afghans, Greeks, Arabs, Mongolians and Turks settled and mingled here, giving deep underlying similarities to Pakistani culture. (3) Social life: the social life of Pakistanis is basically simple and modest; the majority lives in the combined (joint) family system; respect for elders is common to all regional traditions; most people live in villages where farming and livestock are the primary sources of livelihood, while urban employment is in commerce, industrial works and the service sector; marriages are still celebrated in the traditional way and religious festivals are observed with passion and devotion all over the country. (4) Dress: the national dress is simple but graceful; men wear shalwar and qamees or kurta, with traditional caps and pagries as headwear, and women wear shalwar and qamees with a chader (shawl) for headwear; every region has its own style, embroidered dress is popular with women, and every dress follows the norms of modesty and parda. (5) Food: the food is quite simple - wheat bread with vegetables and various pulses is common, and rice with meat is another favourite; the common drinks are milk, lassi, tea, green tea and simple water; richer foods are served at marriages and feasts; in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa meat and green tea are consumed in larger quantities because of the cold weather, in Sindh and Punjab vegetables, milk and dairy products such as yogurt and butter are consumed avidly, and in Balochistan lamb, meat, beef and dry fruits are the favourite food. (6) Arts, crafts and handicrafts: metal crafting, bronze casting, stone carving and seal-making go back to the Indus Valley and Gandhara civilizations; Lahore, Multan, Uch Shareef and Thatta have splendid Islamic architecture; Gujarat is famous for earthenware painting, Peshawar for engraving on bronze, copper and tin, and Balochistan and Punjab for hand-woven carpets and embroidery. (7) Sports and fairs: fairs are held with the changing of seasons, at crop-cutting eve or on occasions in the lives of Sufi saints - famous ones are the Horse and Cattle Show in Lahore, the annual cattle fair at Sibbi in Balochistan and the Shandur Polo Festival at Chitral; wrestling, marksmanship competitions, kabadi and malakhra are the important regional sports. (8) Marriage customs: marriages are celebrated with due pomp and an Islamic touch and are solemnized by Nikkah, though dowry and bride price negatively affect the fabric of society, and the government has promulgated the Jahez Ordinance to overcome this menace. (9) Rites of birth and death: at a birth, sweets are distributed and the Azan is recited in the ears of the newborn; at a death, relatives and neighbours share the grief of the bereaved family and even share the costs of food and drinks for visitors, which develops brotherhood and co-operation.

Q: 3. What do you know about history of national language and write a note on regional languages?

Ans: Urdu, the national language of Pakistan, is a word of Turkish origin meaning 'army'. It developed under Muslim rule in the sub-continent through the interaction of speakers of various dialects, borrowing its vocabulary heavily from Arabic, Persian, Turkish and the regional languages. It is spoken in all four provinces, is highly flexible, deeply influences the regional languages, played a vital role in reflecting the Islamic traditions of the sub-continent's Muslims and spearheaded the Pakistan Movement; the Anjuman-e-Taraqi-e-Urdu, the Urdu Science Board and the National Language Promotion Department promote it, and besides being a link language it is a symbol of national identity. The regional languages are: (1) Pashto: an ancient language spoken widely in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan and parts of Punjab (Mianwali, Attock); deeply influenced by Persian, its script is similar to Arabic; its oldest poem, written in the eighth century, is attributed to Ameer Karor, and Salman Mako wrote Kitab Tarikh-el-Awlia in the thirteenth century; its famous writers are Bayazid Ansari (Pir Rukhan), Khushal Khan Khattak, Rehman Baba and Hamza Shinwari, and the Pashto Academy promotes it. (2) Punjabi: spoken in its true form in northern Punjab, with a rich literary tradition; the Dohay and the mystical poetry of Baba Farid are famous, and its greatest poets are Baba Farid, Bhuley Shah, Sultan Bahu - who wrote mystical (Arifana) poetry in the seventeenth century - and Waris Shah, who composed Heer Ranjha as a masnavi. (3) Sindhi: based on the Sanskrit and Prakrit spoken in Sindh during the Aryan period; after the arrival of Arab traders and conquerors it assimilated a vast Arabic vocabulary and its script changed to Arabic; its famous writers are Shah Abdul Lateef Bhattai, Sachal Sarmast and Abdul Qadir Baidel, and Mirza Qaleech Baig (1853-1929) introduced the modern novel genre into Sindhi and translated several Western literary classics. (4) Balochi: spoken in Balochistan, parts of Dera Ismail Khan in southern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Dera Ghazi Khan in southern Punjab and parts of Sindh; its epic poetry reflects the nomadic lifestyle and glorifies tribal heroes, and its celebrated poets are Mast Tawakkali and Mulla Fazel. (5) Brahui: one of the oldest languages of the Indus Valley region; the Holy Quran has been translated into it, and Malak Daad is among its most famous poets. (6) Hindko: widely spoken in parts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; research shows it predates the Aryan invasion, and a two-thousand-year-old inscription at Taxila is in a language similar to contemporary Hindko; Seraiki, Chitrali, Kohistani and Gojri are also spoken in parts of the province. (7) Kashmiri: spoken in parts of Azad Kashmir, largely by those who migrated from Indian-held Kashmir; its well-known poets are Huba Khatoon, Mehmud Gaami and Armni Laal. (8) Seraiki: widely spoken in Bahawalpur and southern Punjab, the northern parts of Sindh and parts of Dera Ismail Khan district; Khwaja Farid was its famous poet, Sachal Sarmast is also among its greatest poets, and singers Shazia Khushk, Attaullah Khan Eassakhelvi and Abida Perveen have done much to promote it.

Q: 4. Discuss Population, its growth and distribution in Pakistan.

Ans: Pakistan's population has increased about five-fold in 63 years: it was 33 million in 1951, rose to 130.6 million in 1998 and exceeded 170 million in 2010; if the rate of increase continued, it would reach 200 million by 2020. The annual growth rate was about 3.1 percent in 1981 and has decreased to around 1.9 percent. In 1950 Pakistan was the 14th largest country of the world by population, while in 2004 it was the sixth largest. The fast-growing population puts ever-increasing pressure on unemployment, education, health, research, agriculture and civic amenities, and the imbalance between population and resources keeps increasing. As for distribution, about 63.66 percent of the population lives in rural areas and 36.33 percent in urban areas; in 1947 only about 15.4 percent was urban and 84.6 percent rural, so large-scale migration from villages to cities has taken place, and about 60 percent of houses still lack basic amenities like water supply, drainage, electricity and formal latrines, while slums are forming in the cities. The rural population is mostly engaged in agriculture, forming about 51 percent of the working force. By sex the population is 49 percent male and 51 percent female, and by age about 43 percent are up to 14 years old, about 53-54 percent are between 15 and 64 years, and about 3-4 percent are 65 years and above.
